title: Messiah, Hallelujah chorus, in three recordings
question: How much room does each choir leave between Handel’s cries of ‘Hallelujah’?
intro: Handel sets the choir singing together in chords, then passes a tune from one voice to the next. Edison’s Oratorio Chorus recorded it in 1916; Sargent’s performance comes from the Royal Albert Hall in 1926. Scherchen’s fast 1953 account led Owen Jensen, writing in the New Zealand Listener in June 1954, to joke about “Handelian traffic inspectors”.

recordings.label: Oratorio Chorus
recordings.note: Edison’s choir recorded the chorus in 1916, with its accompaniment, on one side of a Diamond Disc released that May.

recordings.label: Malcolm Sargent, Royal Choral Society
recordings.note: A live Royal Albert Hall performance, with the hall’s orchestra accompanying the Royal Choral Society on 2 April 1926.

recordings.label: Hermann Scherchen, London Philharmonic Choir
recordings.note: A quick beat keeps the choral exchanges moving, with the London Symphony Orchestra accompanying a relatively small choir.

passages.label: Orchestral opening and choir entry
passages.note: The violins play the rhythm first. The choir enters three bars later, all four voices singing ‘Hallelujah’ together.

passages.label: “The kingdom of this world”
passages.note: The choir moves together in measured notes above a descending bass. Trumpets and drums fall silent.

passages.label: “King of kings”
passages.note: The sopranos hold their line above the quick answers in the lower voices, then enter higher with each new phrase.

passages.label: Final cadence in D major
passages.note: Choir and orchestra stop. After the rest the choir sings one broad ‘Hallelujah’, ending on a held D-major chord.
